tldr: Real2SimLab has arrived as a unified platform that enables evaluating and training AI (coding agents) that generate simulation programs from real-world videos with only $N + M$ integrations, eliminating the need for $N \times M$ individual implementations.
hero_caption: An overview of this work. It provides an architecture (center) that evaluates state-of-the-art coding agents that write simulation code from videos (left) across diverse benchmarks with official scoring and generates training data via a common interface, alongside a research map organizing nearly 300 related papers (right).
overview:
In robot learning and scene understanding, "real-to-simulation transfer" (building simulation environments from real-world observations such as images and videos) is extremely important. Recently, coding agents powered by large language models have advanced rapidly. A new paradigm has emerged where agents watch real-world videos and automatically generate Python code or Blender scripts that run physics simulations.

However, benchmark fragmentation has stood as a massive barrier. One benchmark evaluates the visual fidelity of generated video frames, another requires a robot action package, and yet another demands 4D object trajectories. Input specifications, deliverables, and scoring pipelines have all been fragmented. As a result, evaluating $N$ methods across $M$ benchmarks required laboriously implementing $N \times M$ custom adapters, making fair cross-method comparisons exceedingly difficult.

To solve this, the authors developed Real2SimLab, a unified platform that adopts the "executable program" submitted by a method as its common interface. By connecting each method and benchmark once via an adapter, seamless interoperability is achieved with just $N + M$ integrations. Furthermore, it features a pipeline that automatically generates reward-annotated training data for reinforcement learning and fine-tuning, while strictly filtering out benchmark test videos via frame matching to avoid data contamination.

Currently, it supports 47 coding agents, 5 non-agent methods, and 6 major benchmarks. Both the platform and Awesome-Real2Sim, a research map of nearly 300 papers, are released as open source.
contributions: Building Real2SimLab, a unified platform that connects diverse video-to-simulation methods and benchmarks through programs as a common standard, enabling collective evaluation with only $N + M$ integrations.

Implementing a sandboxing mechanism that reproduces agent environments, re-executes programs offline, and strictly automates scoring while preserving reproducibility and consistency with official scores.
Providing a training pipeline that detects data contamination caused by video trimming or re-encoding through frame matching to generate clean training data and reward annotations.
Supporting 47 coding agents, 5 baselines, and 6 benchmarks, along with compiling Awesome-Real2Sim, a survey map categorizing nearly 300 papers.

sections.heading: Why Do We Need a Common Platform for Real-to-Sim Evaluation?
sections.summary: AI capable of generating simulation programs from real-world videos has arrived, leading to several benchmarks, but differing input/output specifications caused evaluation overhead to explode. This section explains the motivation and concept behind Real2SimLab, which drastically reduces integration overhead from $N \times M$ to $N + M$ using programs as a common interface.
sections.details:
In robotics and computer vision, real-to-simulation transfer—building simulations from real-world observations—has long been studied. Traditionally, researchers built dedicated, one-off pipelines for each scene, such as fitting an object's mass and friction parameters or reconstructing robot training rooms from 3D scans.

However, recent advances in large models (such as Claude and GPT) have enabled a new paradigm: prompting a coding agent with a video and asking it to "write simulator code that reproduces this phenomenon." For example, given a video of red juice being poured into a glass, the agent autonomously writes code that uses a physics engine to place the glass and fluid and reproduce the pouring behavior. Once turned into a program, users can freely re-render it from arbitrary viewpoints or extract the physical states of objects at any timestep.

Yet, benchmarks measuring this progress were entirely fragmented. Physics-IQ watches the first 3 seconds to predict the following 5 seconds of video frames; Video2World asks for a reconstructed scene and an action package from robot manipulation videos; 4DCodeBench requires a 4D world construction script; and PhysCodeGym requires Blender scenes. Inputs, deliverables, and scoring code were all created independently by separate communities. Consequently, evaluating $N$ methods across $M$ benchmarks required developing $N \times M$ adapters, preventing anyone from conducting cross-benchmark comparisons.

Real2SimLab resolves this by fixing the "program" written by the agent as the common interface. A method author only needs to write one adapter that submits a program, and a benchmark author only needs to write one adapter that maps the task to a common format and invokes the official scorer. This brings the number of integrations down to $N + M$. In addition, it provides a training data generation pipeline that avoids data contamination and a research map called Awesome-Real2Sim summarizing nearly 300 related papers.

captions.F2: The advantages of introducing a shared platform. (a) Previously, dedicated adapters were required for every pair of method and benchmark, requiring $N \times M$ implementations. (b) Real2SimLab uses programs as a common interface, enabling cross-evaluation with only $N + M$ integrations.

sections.heading: Unified Platforms in Other Domains and the Landscape of Real-to-Sim Research
sections.summary: The authors introduce the philosophy of unified evaluation platforms—already successful for language models and robot policies—into the real-to-sim domain, highlighting key differences from prior work. They also outline a survey map categorizing nearly 300 papers by deliverable types.
sections.details:
### Evaluation Platforms in Other Fields vs. This Work
Unified evaluation has already achieved great success across various fields. Examples include lm-evaluation-harness and HELM for language models, VLMEvalKit for multimodal models, SWE-bench and Harbor for software engineering agents, and SIMPLER and XPolicyLab for robot policies. Real2SimLab adopts an adapter pattern similar to XPolicyLab to achieve $N + M$ connectivity, but the underlying artifacts differ fundamentally.

While a robot policy is a "live model" that interacts sequentially with an environment, Real2SimLab deals with a "program" that the agent outputs once at the end of its work. Because a program can be executed standalone at any time, it is decoupled from the agent's interactive trial-and-error session and re-run in a fixed environment to compute scores. Unlike Harbor, which directly validates inside the container where the agent operated, Real2SimLab performs frozen re-runs in an external, independent sandbox.

### A Research Map Categorizing 300 Papers
In Awesome-Real2Sim, released by the authors, nearly 300 papers are categorized based on "what the method produces" and "what the benchmark expects."
- **5 Method Categories**: Physical twins fitting physical parameters (Fitted/Assigned), simulation assets, Scene twins replicating entire environments, Simulation programs calling physics engines, and Learned simulators using neural networks.
- **4 Benchmark Categories**: Those requiring executable simulations, those answering physics questions, those competing on video frame generation, and those validating sim-to-real alignment.

Real2SimLab specifically targets the modern line of coding agents that generate "executable simulation programs." Additionally, drawing on insights from prior work, it incorporates a rigorous frame-matching filtering mechanism to prevent "data contamination" caused by video clips being repurposed across different datasets.

captions.F3: A timeline of the real-to-sim domain derived from Awesome-Real2Sim. Starting from physical parameter estimation, one can clearly observe the recent surge in benchmarks like 4DCodeBench and Video2World that ask coding agents to write simulation code.

sections.heading: Platform Architecture: Sandboxing, Frozen Re-runs, and Unified Scoring
sections.summary: This section covers the core architecture of Real2SimLab. It details the strict physical separation of visible and hidden task data, sandboxed freezing and offline re-runs of deliverables, and the automated scoring pipeline supporting both official scorers and native reproduction metrics.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Task Design and Data Separation
To ensure fair evaluation, each task is physically partitioned into two directories: `visible/` (videos, camera parameters, and scene descriptions visible to the method) and `hidden/` (ground truth deliverables and scoring data). The sandbox running the method never mounts `hidden/`, and validation rules reject invalid references like symlinks. Metadata also specifies required container images, timeouts, and other parameters to automatically generate task instructions for agents.

### 3.2 Method Adapters and Deliverable Conventions
A method adapter only needs to implement a single function: "take `visible/` and return deliverables (a program bundle)." It supports four deliverable conventions, covering major benchmarks:
- **Real2SimLab Convention**: A `solution/run.py` script outputting object trajectories and rendered videos to a designated directory.
- **4DCodeBench Convention**: A 4D world construction script.
- **PhysCodeGym Convention**: A Blender scene file that renders video.
- **Video2World Convention**: A simulation package containing a reconstructed scene and robot actions.

Agents work in an isolated workspace where external access is restricted to model API calls. Self-diagnostic tools are also provided so agents can verify whether running their code twice yields identical results.

### 3.3 Freezing and Offline Re-runs
To measure the capability of the finished program itself rather than an accidental result during the agent's work session, the submitted code is copied, fingerprinted via hashing, and frozen. It is then re-executed in a network-isolated, read-only sandbox (using Docker or rootless bubblewrap). The platform strictly verifies whether running twice with the same seed matches (reproducibility) and whether the re-run matches the output from the working session (session consistency).

### 3.4 Scoring Protocols and Reporting
Two scoring protocols are provided:
- **Native Protocol**: Runs the benchmark's official evaluation code pinned to a specific commit (used for 5 out of 6 benchmarks).
- **Reproduction Protocol**: A custom protocol for cases without official scorers or for scoring user-provided videos. It compares the object trajectory error $e$ against the error of a completely static scene $e_{\text{static}}$, scoring reproduction skill as $\text{skill} = 1 - e / e_{\text{static}}$. It yields 1 for perfect reproduction, 0 for performance matching a static scene, and negative values if worse.

System failures such as machine crashes or container startup failures are logged as infrastructure errors and excluded from method scores, ensuring pure algorithmic performance is compared.

captions.F4: Real2SimLab system architecture. The method adapter on the left and the benchmark adapter on the right connect via the central common task format. Submitted programs are frozen inside a sandbox, and official scoring or reproduction scoring is performed on the output from offline re-runs.

sections.heading: Supported Ecosystem: 47 Agents and 6 Benchmarks
sections.summary: This section outlines the specific agents and benchmarks currently supported by Real2SimLab, validation results against official environments, and plugin extensibility for adding new benchmarks and methods.
sections.details:
### Connecting Diverse Benchmarks
Currently, the platform supports 6 major benchmarks alongside a custom synthetic suite with exact physics:
- **Physics-IQ**: Renders the remaining 5 seconds of video from the first 3 seconds of a real video.
- **Video2World**: Generates scenes and action packages from robot manipulation videos.
- **4DCodeBench**: Generates scripts to build time-evolving 3D scenes (4D worlds).
- **PhysCodeGym**: Generates Blender scenes that reproduce reference videos.
- **PhySimCode**: Estimates simulation code and physical parameters from videos of physical phenomena.
- **IRIS**: Estimates physical parameters from real videos like falling balls (evaluated here via reproduction skill on extracted trajectories).
- **Synthetic suite**: Generates 5 fundamental physical phenomena with exact ground truth: a bouncing ball, a damped pendulum, a sliding block with friction, projectile motion with air resistance, and two-ball collisions.

Each adapter is verified against its upstream repository, confirming that scores match official scorers exactly on Physics-IQ and Video2World (e.g., Push-T tasks).

### 47 Agents and Non-Agent Baselines
Via a bridge to the Harbor framework, 47 agents—including OpenHands, Aider, Cursor CLI, Goose, and Qwen Code—can be executed out of the box. Furthermore, native adapters running directly inside Real2SimLab sandboxes without Harbor are provided for 5 agents: Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, and mini-SWE-agent. 5 simple non-agent baselines are also bundled for comparison.

### Flexible Plugin Design
Benchmarks, methods, evaluation metrics, deliverable formats, and sandbox environments are all modularized as plugins. The repository also includes "Agent skills" designed to let coding agents themselves follow instructions to onboard new benchmarks and methods, facilitating community-driven expansion.

captions.F5: List of the 6 supported benchmarks and the synthetic suite. For each task, the visible inputs, submitted deliverables, and evaluation criteria (official scoring or reproduction skill) are summarized.

sections.heading: Generating RL and Fine-Tuning Data while Preventing Contamination
sections.summary: The authors propose a data generation pipeline to train and improve models, not just evaluate them. This section explains how benchmark test videos are filtered out using motion frame matching to prevent data contamination, and how rewards are annotated using the exact same evaluation code.
sections.details:
### The Serious Challenge of Data Contamination
High benchmark performance can often be misleading if test videos were accidentally included in training data. In real-to-sim transfer, researchers frequently repurpose public web videos, creating a constant risk that resized, re-encoded, or cropped versions of the same event leak across datasets.

### Rigorous Deduplication via Frame Matching
Real2SimLab incorporates an automated deduplication check when generating training tasks. Moving frames are downscaled into small thumbnails and exhaustively compared across temporal offsets. This detects identical footage even across resolution changes, lighting variations, frame rate drops, or spatial crops. In tests, it accurately detected 36 out of 40 synthetic evaluation video copies (missing only extremely compressed clips), and automatically identified and removed all 27 clips that PhysCodeGym had reused from Physics-IQ in real data.

### Reward Annotation and Training Applications
After an agent writes a program for a clean, deduplicated video, the pipeline computes a "reward" (Reproduction skill score) using the exact same scoring code used during evaluation. Infrastructure failures like container crashes are treated as missing values rather than zero rewards, clearly distinguishing algorithm failures from environment glitches.

Sets of "video, program, reward score, and agent thought trace" generated this way can be used for supervised fine-tuning on high-reward programs or preference learning like DPO. Furthermore, because a scalar reward is returned immediately for an entire program, it can serve directly as a reward model for modern online reinforcement learning algorithms such as GRPO or RLOO. When evaluating trained models, thumbnails of training videos are retained to re-verify that evaluation data has not been contaminated.

captions.F6: The training data creation pipeline. Candidate training tasks (left) are checked against evaluation videos via thumbnail comparison on moving frames, filtering out duplicates (center). For remaining clean tasks, programs are generated and annotated with rewards using the exact evaluation code to form datasets (right).

sections.heading: Toward an Open Real-to-Sim Ecosystem
sections.summary: This section summarizes the contributions, highlighting how Real2SimLab accelerates research cycles and inviting the community to build together via "Real2SimHub."
sections.details:
In this paper, the authors presented Real2SimLab, a unified platform for real-to-simulation transfer from real-world videos. By establishing agent-generated programs as a common interface, the platform reduces integration costs from $N \times M$ to $N + M$, enabling cross-evaluation of 6 major benchmarks and 47 agents with single-command simplicity.

Furthermore, by establishing a clean training data generation and reward annotation pipeline that detects video overlap to prevent data contamination, the paper provides a foundation for future fine-tuning and reinforcement learning research. The authors also compiled Awesome-Real2Sim, a research map organizing nearly 300 papers.

Both the platform and research map are open source. The authors invite the global research community to contribute methods, benchmarks, and real-world video tasks via the open "Real2SimHub" community.

takeaways: Real-to-sim evaluation—generating simulation code from videos—can now be cross-compared with simple $N+M$ integrations by using executable programs as a common interface.
Decoupling the program from the agent's work session and conducting "frozen offline re-runs" in a fixed environment is key to fair, reproducible scoring.
Because public video datasets frequently share source clips, rigorous contamination checks via thumbnail frame matching are essential.
Using identical execution and scoring code to mass-produce reward-annotated data allows the platform to be directly utilized as an RL environment (e.g., GRPO) for coding agents.
limitations: This paper focuses primarily on platform design and validation; large-scale empirical comparison experiments across all 47 supported agents remain future work.
Video copies subjected to extreme compression or severe geometric transformations may still occasionally slip past the contamination detection filter.
Because no current real-to-sim benchmark provides official training splits, training data generation currently relies mostly on the synthetic suite or user-supplied videos.
